claim: A large fraction of human cancers contain genetic alterations within the Mitogen Activated Protein Kinase (MAPK) signaling network.
source: A large fraction of human cancers contain genetic alterations within the Mitogen Activated Protein Kinase (MAPK) signaling network that promote unpredictable phenotypes.
evidence: This is a general statement about cancer genetics that is supported by the citation to Sanchez-Vega et al., 2018 in the introduction.

claim: The temporal patterns of MAPK activity (i.e. signaling dynamics) differentially regulate cell behavior.
source: Previous studies have shown that the temporal patterns of MAPK activity (i.e. signaling dynamics) differentially regulate cell behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations in the introduction to multiple studies on signaling dynamics.

claim: Oncogene expression leads to either pulsatile or sustained ERK activity.
source: Here, we show that oncogene expression leads to either pulsatile or sustained ERK activity that correlate with opposing cellular behaviors (i.e. proliferation vs. cell cycle arrest, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: Pulsatile ERK activity correlates with proliferation.
source: Here, we show that oncogene expression leads to either pulsatile or sustained ERK activity that correlate with opposing cellular behaviors (i.e. proliferation vs. cell cycle arrest, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1D showing increased S-phase in cells with pulsatile ERK activity.

claim: Sustained ERK activity correlates with cell cycle arrest.
source: Here, we show that oncogene expression leads to either pulsatile or sustained ERK activity that correlate with opposing cellular behaviors (i.e. proliferation vs. cell cycle arrest, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1D showing decreased S-phase in cells with sustained ERK activity.

claim: Sustained ERK activity triggers ERK activity waves in unperturbed neighboring cells.
source: Moreover, sustained–but not pulsatile–ERK activity triggers ERK activity waves in unperturbed neighboring cells that depend on the membrane metalloprotease ADAM17 and EGFR activity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2 showing ERK waves in neighboring cells.

claim: ERK activity waves in neighboring cells depend on ADAM17.
source: Moreover, sustained–but not pulsatile–ERK activity triggers ERK activity waves in unperturbed neighboring cells that depend on the membrane metalloprotease ADAM17 and EGFR activity.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3 showing that ADAM17 knockout abolishes ERK waves.

claim: ERK activity waves in neighboring cells depend on EGFR activity.
source: Moreover, sustained–but not pulsatile–ERK activity triggers ERK activity waves in unperturbed neighboring cells that depend on the membrane metalloprotease ADAM17 and EGFR activity.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3E showing that EGFR inhibition blocks ERK waves.

claim: The ADAM17-EGFR signaling axis coordinates neighboring cell migration toward oncogenic cells.
source: Interestingly, the ADAM17-EGFR signaling axis coordinates neighboring cell migration toward oncogenic cells and is required for oncogenic cell extrusion.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5A showing directed migration that is blocked by ADAM17 knockout or EGFR inhibition.

claim: The ADAM17-EGFR signaling axis is required for oncogenic cell extrusion.
source: Interestingly, the ADAM17-EGFR signaling axis coordinates neighboring cell migration toward oncogenic cells and is required for oncogenic cell extrusion.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5D-E showing that ADAM17 knockout or EGFR inhibition prevents extrusion.

claim: The temporal patterns of MAPK activity differentially regulate cell autonomous and non-cell autonomous effects of oncogene expression.
source: Overall, our data suggests that the temporal patterns of MAPK activity differentially regulate cell autonomous and non-cell autonomous effects of oncogene expression.
evidence: This is the main conclusion supported by all experimental data showing different effects of pulsatile vs sustained ERK activity.

claim: The RTK/RAS/ERK signaling axis is mutated in most human cancers.
source: The Receptor-Tyrosine Kinase (RTK)/RAS/ERK signaling axis (Figure 1A) is mutated in most human cancers (Sanchez-Vega et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sanchez-Vega et al., 2018.

claim: The ERK pathway promotes proliferation, differentiation, survival and cell migration in normal conditions.
source: In normal conditions, the ERK pathway promotes proliferation, differentiation, survival and cell migration (Johnson and Lapadat, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Johnson and Lapadat, 2002.

claim: Mutations or amplification of ERK pathway components can promote oncogene-induced senescence during oncogenesis.
source: During oncogenesis, mutations or amplification of ERK pathway components can also promote oncogene-induced senescence (Hahn and Weinberg, 2002) (OIS) or oncogenic cell extrusion from epithelial monolayers in the so-called Epithelial Defense Against Cancer response (EDAC) (Hogan et al., 2009; Kajita et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hahn and Weinberg, 2002.

claim: Mutations or amplification of ERK pathway components can promote oncogenic cell extrusion from epithelial monolayers in the Epithelial Defense Against Cancer response (EDAC).
source: During oncogenesis, mutations or amplification of ERK pathway components can also promote oncogene-induced senescence (Hahn and Weinberg, 2002) (OIS) or oncogenic cell extrusion from epithelial monolayers in the so-called Epithelial Defense Against Cancer response (EDAC) (Hogan et al., 2009; Kajita et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hogan et al., 2009 and Kajita et al., 2010.

claim: Pulsatile or sustained ERK activity have different effects on cell behavior.
source: In fact, in vivo and in vitro studies have now shown that pulsatile or sustained ERK activity have different effects on cell behavior (Albeck et al., 2013; Aoki et al., 2013; de la Cova et al., 2017; Johnson and Toettcher, 2019; Santos et al., 2007; Bugaj et al., 2018; Aoki et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies on ERK dynamics.

claim: MCF10A cells were transduced with lentiviral vectors expressing ERK KTR-mCerulean3 and ERK-mRuby2.
source: MCF10A cells were transduced with lentiviral vectors expressing ERK KTR-mCerulean3 and ERK-mRuby2.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1 legend and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The doxycycline inducible system (rTtA and TRE3G) was used to drive the expression of oncogenes during live imaging.
source: The doxycycline inducible system (rTtA and TRE3G) was used to drive the expression of oncogenes during live imaging.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1 legend and shown schematically in Figure 1B.

claim: EGFR overexpression leads to increased frequency of ERK activity pulses with no change in ERK kinase localization.
source: Our results revealed two qualitatively different responses to oncogene induction: (i) increased frequency of ERK activity pulses with no change in ERK kinase localization (i.e. EGFR, B-RafWT), and (ii) sustained ERK activity with subsequent nuclear translocation of ERK kinase (i.e. B-RafV600E, MEK2DD) (Figure 1, and Figure 1—Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: B-RafWT overexpression leads to increased frequency of ERK activity pulses with no change in ERK kinase localization.
source: Our results revealed two qualitatively different responses to oncogene induction: (i) increased frequency of ERK activity pulses with no change in ERK kinase localization (i.e. EGFR, B-RafWT), and (ii) sustained ERK activity with subsequent nuclear translocation of ERK kinase (i.e. B-RafV600E, MEK2DD) (Figure 1, and Figure 1—Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: B-RafV600E overexpression leads to sustained ERK activity with subsequent nuclear translocation of ERK kinase.
source: Our results revealed two qualitatively different responses to oncogene induction: (i) increased frequency of ERK activity pulses with no change in ERK kinase localization (i.e. EGFR, B-RafWT), and (ii) sustained ERK activity with subsequent nuclear translocation of ERK kinase (i.e. B-RafV600E, MEK2DD) (Figure 1, and Figure 1—Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: MEK2DD overexpression leads to sustained ERK activity with subsequent nuclear translocation of ERK kinase.
source: Our results revealed two qualitatively different responses to oncogene induction: (i) increased frequency of ERK activity pulses with no change in ERK kinase localization (i.e. EGFR, B-RafWT), and (ii) sustained ERK activity with subsequent nuclear translocation of ERK kinase (i.e. B-RafV600E, MEK2DD) (Figure 1, and Figure 1—Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: MEK1/2WT expression is capable of exporting ERK into the cytoplasm without changing kinase activity.
source: Of note, MEK1/2WT expression is capable of exporting ERK into the cytoplasm without changing kinase activity (Adachi et al., 2000; Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and ERK nuclear accumulation occurs only when activity is sustained, suggesting that ERK activity and ERK localization are not always correlated.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Adachi et al., 2000 and data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: ERK nuclear accumulation occurs only when activity is sustained.
source: Of note, MEK1/2WT expression is capable of exporting ERK into the cytoplasm without changing kinase activity (Adachi et al., 2000; Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and ERK nuclear accumulation occurs only when activity is sustained, suggesting that ERK activity and ERK localization are not always correlated.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: ERK activity and ERK localization are not always correlated.
source: Of note, MEK1/2WT expression is capable of exporting ERK into the cytoplasm without changing kinase activity (Adachi et al., 2000; Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and ERK nuclear accumulation occurs only when activity is sustained, suggesting that ERK activity and ERK localization are not always correlated.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that MEK1/2WT can change localization without changing activity.

claim: B-RafWT and B-RafV600E show similar expression levels by immunoblotting.
source: Interestingly, expression of B-RafWT or B-RafV600E elicit qualitatively different downstream dynamics even though they differ in a single amino acid and show similar expression levels by immunoblotting (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: B-RafV600E is insensitive to negative feedback regulation by ERK.
source: Given that the B-RafV600E is insensitive to negative feedback regulation by ERK (Yao et al., 2015), this result suggests that ERK inhibition to B-RafWT is mechanistically involved in the characteristic pulsatile dynamics.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yao et al., 2015.

claim: ERK inhibition to B-RafWT is mechanistically involved in the characteristic pulsatile dynamics.
source: Given that the B-RafV600E is insensitive to negative feedback regulation by ERK (Yao et al., 2015), this result suggests that ERK inhibition to B-RafWT is mechanistically involved in the characteristic pulsatile dynamics.
evidence: This is inferred from the difference in dynamics between B-RafWT and B-RafV600E and the known feedback regulation.

claim: Pulsatile ERK dynamics consistently correlated with increased cell cycle progression.
source: Next, we assessed how ERK dynamics affect cell behaviors by measuring cell migration and proliferation. While pulsatile ERK dynamics (i.e. EGFR or B-RafWT) consistently correlated with increased cell cycle progression, sustained ERK activity (i.e. B-RafV600E or MEK2DD) caused cell cycle arrest and increased migration (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1D showing increased S-phase for pulsatile ERK conditions.

claim: Sustained ERK activity caused cell cycle arrest and increased migration.
source: Next, we assessed how ERK dynamics affect cell behaviors by measuring cell migration and proliferation. While pulsatile ERK dynamics (i.e. EGFR or B-RafWT) consistently correlated with increased cell cycle progression, sustained ERK activity (i.e. B-RafV600E or MEK2DD) caused cell cycle arrest and increased migration (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1D showing decreased S-phase and increased migration for sustained ERK conditions.

claim: Observed differences in cell behavior correlated with dynamics independently of the point in the cascade that perturbations were introduced.
source: Importantly, observed differences in cell behavior correlated with dynamics independently of the point in the cascade that perturbations were introduced (EGFR, Raf or MEK), suggesting that ERK is responsible for differences in cell behaviors rather than alternate downstream pathways.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that perturbations at different levels of the cascade show similar dynamics-dependent behaviors.

claim: ERK is responsible for differences in cell behaviors rather than alternate downstream pathways.
source: Importantly, observed differences in cell behavior correlated with dynamics independently of the point in the cascade that perturbations were introduced (EGFR, Raf or MEK), suggesting that ERK is responsible for differences in cell behaviors rather than alternate downstream pathways.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that perturbations at different cascade levels show similar dynamics-dependent behaviors.

claim: Expression of B-RafWT or B-RafV600E caused different ERK activity dynamics and triggered opposing cellular behaviors.
source: Moreover, expression of B-RafWT or B-RafV600E, which activate the cascade at the same point, caused different ERK activity dynamics (i.e. pulsatile or sustained respectively) and triggered opposing cellular behaviors (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: ERK activity dynamics can either promote or inhibit proliferation cell autonomously.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that ERK activity dynamics can either promote or inhibit proliferation cell autonomously.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that pulsatile ERK promotes proliferation while sustained ERK inhibits it.

claim: At 24 hr post-oncogene expression, cells retain E-Cad expression with no clear increase in N-Cad.
source: While cell migration was clearly increased at 24 hr post-oncogene expression, cells retain E-Cad expression with no clear increase in N-Cad, as was observed in TGFβ-induced EMT (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Altered cell behaviors at the studied time points are either distinct from or precede those resulting from EMT.
source: These results indicate that at the time points studied here, altered cell behaviors are either distinct from or precede those resulting from EMT.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that cells show increased migration without EMT markers.

claim: Expression of B-RafV600E, but not B-RafWT, resulted in waves of ERK activation of neighboring cells.
source: Interestingly, expression of B-RafV600E, but not B-RafWT, resulted in waves of ERK activation of neighboring cells (Figure 2B–C and Figure 2—Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2B-C showing ERK waves only with B-RafV600E.

claim: Oncogenic perturbations that elicit sustained ERK activity propagate ERK activity pulses to neighboring cells.
source: This comparison suggests that oncogenic perturbations that elicit sustained ERK activity propagate ERK activity pulses to neighboring cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that sustained but not pulsatile ERK triggers waves in neighbors.

claim: Other oncogenes that triggered sustained, but not pulsatile, ERK activity also promoted ERK activity waves in the neighboring cells.
source: In agreement, other oncogenes that triggered sustained, but not pulsatile, ERK activity also promoted ERK activity waves in the neighboring cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Neighboring epithelia did not activate p38 or JNK MAPK pathways.
source: By using KTRs for p38 and JNK, we observed that neighboring epithelia did not activate other the MAPK pathways (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C showing no p38 or JNK activation.

claim: Spontaneous cell death events were followed by similar ERK signaling waves.
source: Notably, spontaneous cell death events were also followed by similar ERK signaling waves (Figure 2—Video 2), indicating that oncogene expression and cell death may be similarly perceived by neighboring cells.
evidence: This is supported by observation in Figure 2—Video 2.

claim: Oncogene expression and cell death may be similarly perceived by neighboring cells.
source: Notably, spontaneous cell death events were also followed by similar ERK signaling waves (Figure 2—Video 2), indicating that oncogene expression and cell death may be similarly perceived by neighboring cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both oncogene expression and cell death trigger ERK waves.

claim: ERK waves in epithelial monolayers depend on the membrane-tethered sheddase ADAM17.
source: Previous studies demonstrated that ERK waves in epithelial monolayers depend on the membrane-tethered sheddase ADAM17, which releases membrane-bound growth factors that activate EGFR signaling in adjacent cells (Aoki et al., 2013; Aoki et al., 2017; Hiratsuka et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: ADAM17 releases membrane-bound growth factors that activate EGFR signaling in adjacent cells.
source: Previous studies demonstrated that ERK waves in epithelial monolayers depend on the membrane-tethered sheddase ADAM17, which releases membrane-bound growth factors that activate EGFR signaling in adjacent cells (Aoki et al., 2013; Aoki et al., 2017; Hiratsuka et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: ADAM17 is necessary in inducible, but not neighboring cells, to trigger ERK waves in the monolayer.
source: Live imaging of WT and ADAM17KO cocultures indicated that ADAM17 is necessary in inducible, but not neighboring cells, to trigger ERK waves in the monolayer (Figure 3B–C and Figure 2—Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3B-C showing that ADAM17 knockout in inducible cells blocks waves.

claim: ADAM17 decodes ERK activity dynamics in inducible cells to transmit ERK signaling to neighboring cells.
source: Therefore, ADAM17 decodes ERK activity dynamics in inducible cells to transmit ERK signaling to neighboring cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ADAM17 is required in inducible cells for waves.

claim: ADAM17 is weakly phosphorylated compared to other ERK substrates.
source: Previous work has shown that ADAM17 is weakly phosphorylated compared to other ERK substrates (Díaz-Rodríguez et al., 2002), thus the phosphorylation-dephosphorylation kinetics of ADAM17 and the temporal patterns of ERK activity may explain dynamics-specific ADAM17 activation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Díaz-Rodríguez et al., 2002.

claim: The phosphorylation-dephosphorylation kinetics of ADAM17 and the temporal patterns of ERK activity may explain dynamics-specific ADAM17 activation.
source: Previous work has shown that ADAM17 is weakly phosphorylated compared to other ERK substrates (Díaz-Rodríguez et al., 2002), thus the phosphorylation-dephosphorylation kinetics of ADAM17 and the temporal patterns of ERK activity may explain dynamics-specific ADAM17 activation.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on known ADAM17 phosphorylation properties.

claim: ADAM17-released growth factors include HB-EGF, TGF-α, Epiregulin, and Amphiregulin.
source: ADAM17-released growth factors include HB-EGF, TGF-α, Epiregulin, and Amphiregulin (Zunke and Rose-John, 2017; Rios-Doria et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zunke and Rose-John, 2017 and Rios-Doria et al., 2015.

claim: Amphiregulin (AREG) was the most upregulated, ADAM17-dependent protein in the supernatant.
source: Of note, the EGFR ligand Amphiregulin (AREG) was the most upregulated, ADAM17-dependent protein in the supernatant, suggesting that AREG released from inducible cells could act as an oncogene-dependent paracrine signaling molecule.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: AREG released from inducible cells could act as an oncogene-dependent paracrine signaling molecule.
source: Of note, the EGFR ligand Amphiregulin (AREG) was the most upregulated, ADAM17-dependent protein in the supernatant, suggesting that AREG released from inducible cells could act as an oncogene-dependent paracrine signaling molecule.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that AREG is highly upregulated in an ADAM17-dependent manner.

claim: Cocultures pre-incubated with AREG function-blocking antibodies or EGFR inhibitors prevented neighboring cell ERK activation without affecting ERK signaling in inducible cells.
source: Accordingly, cocultures pre-incubated with AREG function-blocking antibodies or EGFR inhibitors prevented neighboring cell ERK activation without affecting ERK signaling in inducible cells (Figure 3E–F).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3E-F showing blocked waves with AREG antibody or EGFR inhibitor.

claim: Oncogene-dependent ERK waves are mediated by ADAM17 (in inducible cells), AREG release, and EGFR signaling.
source: These results indicate that oncogene-dependent ERK waves are mediated by ADAM17 (in inducible cells), AREG release, and EGFR signaling (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3 showing the requirement for ADAM17, AREG, and EGFR.

claim: Sustained ERK signaling in inducible cells increased proliferation of neighboring cells up to 10-fold.
source: Accordingly, sustained ERK signaling in inducible cells increased proliferation of neighboring cells up to 10-fold (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is supported by EdU incorporation data in Figure 4.

claim: Depending on ERK dynamics, oncogenic cells can have either cell autonomous or non-cell autonomous contributions to tissue growth.
source: Together, these data indicate that, depending on ERK dynamics, oncogenic cells can have either cell autonomous or non-cell autonomous contributions to tissue growth.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that pulsatile ERK promotes cell-autonomous proliferation while sustained ERK promotes non-cell autonomous proliferation.

claim: ERK waves have been shown to orient collective cell migration during wound healing.
source: In addition to proliferation, ERK waves have been shown to orient collective cell migration during wound healing (Aoki et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Aoki et al., 2017.

claim: Sustained ERK activity in B-RafV600E-inducible cells correlated with neighboring cell migration towards inducible cells in an ADAM17 and EGFR-dependent manner.
source: In cocultures, sustained ERK activity in B-RafV600E-inducible cells correlated with neighboring cell migration towards inducible cells in an ADAM17 and EGFR-dependent manner (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5A showing directed migration that is blocked by ADAM17 knockout or EGFR inhibition.

claim: Pulsatile ERK activity was not sufficient to extrude cells.
source: Interestingly, while pulsatile ERK activity (i.e. EGFR and B-Raf) was not sufficient to extrude cells, sustained ERK activity (i.e. B-RafV600E and MEK2DD) led to efficient epithelial cell extrusion apically (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5C showing no extrusion with pulsatile ERK.

claim: Sustained ERK activity led to efficient epithelial cell extrusion apically.
source: Interestingly, while pulsatile ERK activity (i.e. EGFR and B-Raf) was not sufficient to extrude cells, sustained ERK activity (i.e. B-RafV600E and MEK2DD) led to efficient epithelial cell extrusion apically (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5C showing extrusion with sustained ERK.

claim: KRASG12V induction did not result in apical extrusion to the extent observed for HRASG12V.
source: KRASG12V induction did not result in apical extrusion to the extent observed for HRASG12V (Hogan et al., 2009, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and citation to Hogan et al., 2009.

claim: Apical extrusion occurs when oncogenic perturbations trigger sustained ERK activity.
source: Taken together, our data suggests that apical extrusion occurs when oncogenic perturbations trigger sustained ERK activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that only sustained ERK activity leads to extrusion.

claim: Cells with sustained ERK activity were fully extruded, sitting above WT cells in the plane of the monolayer.
source: To differentiate between pseudostratified or de-laminated (Grieve and Rabouille, 2014) epithelium and extrusion we analyzed confocal images of E-cad membrane staining in induced cocultures. Cells with sustained ERK activity were fully extruded, sitting above WT cells in the plane of the monolayer (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by confocal imaging data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: E-Cad is maintained at the junctions between WT cells below extruded cells.
source: These images also demonstrate maintenance of E-Cad at the junctions between WT cells below extruded cells.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The majority of oncogenic cells were extruded from 4 to 8 hr after induction.
source: Quantification of fully-extruded cells at several timepoints showed the majority of oncogenic cells being extruded from 4 to 8 hr after induction, but continuing until 24 hr, when 91% of inducible cells are fully extruded.
evidence: This is supported by quantification data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: 91% of inducible cells are fully extruded at 24 hr after induction.
source: Quantification of fully-extruded cells at several timepoints showed the majority of oncogenic cells being extruded from 4 to 8 hr after induction, but continuing until 24 hr, when 91% of inducible cells are fully extruded.
evidence: This is supported by quantification data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Transient accumulation of actin at the basal interface of B-RafV600E expressing and neighboring cells first closed off the basal attachments of inducible cells before they were pushed apically out of the monolayer.
source: Using this tool, we observed transient accumulation of actin at the basal interface of B-RafV600E expressing and neighboring cells that first closed off the basal attachments of inducible cells before they were pushed apically out of the monolayer (Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and Figure 5—Video 2).
evidence: This is supported by live actin imaging data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and Figure 5—Video 2.

claim: Polarized, actin-containing basal protrusions were dependent on EGFR activity.
source: These polarized, actin-containing basal protrusions were dependent on EGFR activity as they could be inhibited by EGFR inhibitor.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D showing reduced actin enrichment with EGFR inhibitor.

claim: Apoptotic extrusion relies on Sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) signaling through intrinsic S1P production and juxtracrine activation of the GPCR S1PR2.
source: Apoptotic extrusion relies on Sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) signaling through intrinsic S1P production and juxtracrine activation of the GPCR S1PR2 (Gu et al., 2011), yet inhibition of S1P production had only moderate effects on apical extrusion of MEK2DD cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gu et al., 2011.

claim: Inhibition of S1P production had only moderate effects on apical extrusion of MEK2DD cells.
source: Apoptotic extrusion relies on Sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) signaling through intrinsic S1P production and juxtracrine activation of the GPCR S1PR2 (Gu et al., 2011), yet inhibition of S1P production had only moderate effects on apical extrusion of MEK2DD cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2G.

claim: The apical extrusion of oncogenic cells observed in these experiments are similar to the EDAC mechanism previously described for HRASG12V, V-Src, and other cells.
source: Together, our results suggest that the apical extrusion of oncogenic cells observed in our experiments are similar to the EDAC mechanism previously described for HRASG12V, V-Src, and other cells (Hogan et al., 2009; Kajita et al., 2010; Kajita and Fujita, 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from similarities between the observed extrusion and previously described EDAC.

claim: Extrusion of inducible cells was abolished by ADAM17KO, EGFR inhibition, or AREG function-blocking antibodies.
source: To test the role of ADAM17-mediated AREG-EGFR paracrine signals in promoting extrusion, we performed extrusion assays using ADAM17KO cells or in the presence of EGFR inhibitor or AREG function-blocking antibodies. Extrusion of inducible cells was abolished in these conditions (Figure 5D–G), suggesting that ERK signaling waves are required for extrusion.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5D-G showing no extrusion with these interventions.

claim: ERK signaling waves are required for extrusion.
source: To test the role of ADAM17-mediated AREG-EGFR paracrine signals in promoting extrusion, we performed extrusion assays using ADAM17KO cells or in the presence of EGFR inhibitor or AREG function-blocking antibodies. Extrusion of inducible cells was abolished in these conditions (Figure 5D–G), suggesting that ERK signaling waves are required for extrusion.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that blocking the wave mechanism prevents extrusion.

claim: Activation of inducible cells alone is not sufficient for extrusion, but neighboring cell ERK activation may be required.
source: Of note, since ADAM17KO and EGFR inhibition affect ERK activation of neighboring cells without altering ERK dynamics in inducible cells, we hypothesized that that activation of inducible cells alone is not sufficient for extrusion, but that neighboring cell ERK activation may be required.
evidence: This is hypothesized based on the observation that blocking neighbor ERK activation prevents extrusion.

claim: The stress MAPK p38 phosphorylates and activates ADAM17.
source: Previous studies have shown that the stress MAPK p38 phosphorylates and activates ADAM17 (Xu and Derynck, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Xu and Derynck, 2010.

claim: p38 activation leads to ERK signaling waves.
source: As expected, we found that p38 activation leads to ERK signaling waves (Figure 6A–B), proliferation (Xu and Derynck, 2010; Figure 6—figure supplement 2), directed migration (Figure 6C) and extrusion in an ADAM17 and EGFR dependent manner (Figure 6D and Figure 6—Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6A-B showing ERK waves with MKK3DD expression.

claim: p38 activation leads to proliferation.
source: As expected, we found that p38 activation leads to ERK signaling waves (Figure 6A–B), proliferation (Xu and Derynck, 2010; Figure 6—figure supplement 2), directed migration (Figure 6C) and extrusion in an ADAM17 and EGFR dependent manner (Figure 6D and Figure 6—Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2 and citation to Xu and Derynck, 2010.

claim: p38 activation leads to directed migration.
source: As expected, we found that p38 activation leads to ERK signaling waves (Figure 6A–B), proliferation (Xu and Derynck, 2010; Figure 6—figure supplement 2), directed migration (Figure 6C) and extrusion in an ADAM17 and EGFR dependent manner (Figure 6D and Figure 6—Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6C showing directed migration with MKK3DD.

claim: p38 activation leads to extrusion in an ADAM17 and EGFR dependent manner.
source: As expected, we found that p38 activation leads to ERK signaling waves (Figure 6A–B), proliferation (Xu and Derynck, 2010; Figure 6—figure supplement 2), directed migration (Figure 6C) and extrusion in an ADAM17 and EGFR dependent manner (Figure 6D and Figure 6—Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6D showing extrusion with MKK3DD that is blocked by ADAM17 knockout or EGFR inhibition.

claim: B-RafV600E oncogenic signaling, extrusion and proliferation were unaffected by p38 inhibition.
source: However, B-RafV600E oncogenic signaling, extrusion and proliferation were unaffected by p38 inhibition (Figure 6—figure supplement 3), suggesting that sustained ERK or p38 activity are each capable of activating ADAM17 paracrine signaling.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: Sustained ERK or p38 activity are each capable of activating ADAM17 paracrine signaling.
source: However, B-RafV600E oncogenic signaling, extrusion and proliferation were unaffected by p38 inhibition (Figure 6—figure supplement 3), suggesting that sustained ERK or p38 activity are each capable of activating ADAM17 paracrine signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that p38 inhibition doesn't affect B-RafV600E-induced extrusion.

claim: MEK inhibition decreased directed migration and prevented extrusion in MKK3DD cocultures.
source: Using this ERK-independent MKK3DD extrusion system, we found that MEK inhibition decreased directed migration and prevented extrusion, confirming that extrusion requires ERK activity in the neighboring cells (Figure 6C–D).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6C-D showing that MEK inhibition blocks migration and extrusion.

claim: Extrusion requires ERK activity in the neighboring cells.
source: Using this ERK-independent MKK3DD extrusion system, we found that MEK inhibition decreased directed migration and prevented extrusion, confirming that extrusion requires ERK activity in the neighboring cells (Figure 6C–D).
evidence: This is confirmed by the observation that MEK inhibition in the MKK3DD system blocks extrusion.

claim: ERK activity is required for extrusion in both oncogenic and neighboring cells with qualitatively different temporal dynamics.
source: Thus, ERK activity is required for extrusion in both oncogenic and neighboring cells with qualitatively different temporal dynamics.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that sustained ERK in oncogenic cells and pulsatile ERK in neighbors are both required.

claim: Inhibition of S1P signaling in MKK3DD cocultures reduced extrusion efficiency despite having unaffected signaling.
source: Notably, inhibition of S1P signaling in MKK3DD cocultures also reduced extrusion efficiency despite having unaffected signaling (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: Cell-autonomous ERK or p38 activation in extruded cells may underlie the fundamental differences reported between extrusion of oncogenic and stressed cells.
source: This result suggests that cell-autonomous ERK or p38 activation in extruded cells may underlie the fundamental differences reported between extrusion of oncogenic and stressed cells.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the differential effects of S1P inhibition.

claim: The proportion of inducible cells was inversely correlated with extrusion efficiency.
source: We first tested the efficiency of extrusion with altered proportions of B-RafV600E cells in the coculture, as higher proportions will have de-centralized and overlapping signaling events. The proportion of inducible cells was inversely correlated with extrusion efficiency (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 7A showing decreased extrusion with higher proportions of oncogenic cells.

claim: Exogenous addition of AREG eliminated directed migration of neighboring cells and extrusion.
source: Moreover, exogenous addition of AREG, which triggers widespread ERK activation preventing any spatially defined waves, eliminated directed migration of neighboring cells and extrusion (Figure 7B–C).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 7B-C showing loss of directed migration and extrusion with AREG addition.

claim: Growth factor signaling provides directional information during extrusion.
source: The observation that in cocultures, polarized actin enrichment in neighboring cell basal protrusions is absent with EGFR inhibition, also indicates that growth factor signaling provides directional information during extrusion (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that EGFR inhibition eliminates polarized actin enrichment.

claim: Locally generated paracrine signaling coordinates directed migration of neighboring epithelia to promote extrusion of oncogenic cells.
source: Together this data suggests that locally generated paracrine signaling coordinates directed migration of neighboring epithelia to promote extrusion of oncogenic cells (Figure 8).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that disrupting spatial gradients prevents directed migration and extrusion.

claim: Different ERK pathway oncogenes trigger two distinct temporal patterns: pulsatile or sustained ERK activity.
source: To better understand the signaling effects of oncogenic mutations, we used live cell imaging of signaling biosensors upon induction of oncogenes and found that different ERK pathway oncogenes trigger two distinct temporal patterns: pulsatile or sustained ERK activity.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1 showing two distinct dynamics patterns.

claim: Pulsatile ERK activity correlates with increased proliferation.
source: While our approach is admittedly different than acquisition of point mutations in vivo, ERK dynamics resulting from oncogene overexpression robustly correlated with the same cellular phenotypes: (i) pulsatile ERK activity correlates with increased proliferation and, (ii) sustained ERK activity leads to cell cycle arrest similar to OIS (Hahn and Weinberg, 2002; Courtois-Cox et al., 2006; Kuilman et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1D and citations to OIS literature.

claim: Sustained ERK activity leads to cell cycle arrest similar to OIS.
source: While our approach is admittedly different than acquisition of point mutations in vivo, ERK dynamics resulting from oncogene overexpression robustly correlated with the same cellular phenotypes: (i) pulsatile ERK activity correlates with increased proliferation and, (ii) sustained ERK activity leads to cell cycle arrest similar to OIS (Hahn and Weinberg, 2002; Courtois-Cox et al., 2006; Kuilman et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1D and citations to OIS literature.

claim: Sustained ERK activity in oncogenic cells triggers ERK signaling waves through unperturbed neighboring cells that depend on the ADAM17-EGFR paracrine signaling axis.
source: Moreover, we showed that sustained ERK activity in oncogenic cells triggers ERK signaling waves through unperturbed neighboring cells. These signaling waves depend on the ADAM17-EGFR paracrine signaling axis and lead to different non cell-autonomous behaviors such as (i) proliferation, (ii) directed migration of neighboring cells toward oncogenic cells, and (iii) oncogenic cell extrusion (Figure 8).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: ERK signaling waves lead to proliferation of neighboring cells.
source: Moreover, we showed that sustained ERK activity in oncogenic cells triggers ERK signaling waves through unperturbed neighboring cells. These signaling waves depend on the ADAM17-EGFR paracrine signaling axis and lead to different non cell-autonomous behaviors such as (i) proliferation, (ii) directed migration of neighboring cells toward oncogenic cells, and (iii) oncogenic cell extrusion (Figure 8).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: ERK signaling waves lead to directed migration of neighboring cells toward oncogenic cells.
source: Moreover, we showed that sustained ERK activity in oncogenic cells triggers ERK signaling waves through unperturbed neighboring cells. These signaling waves depend on the ADAM17-EGFR paracrine signaling axis and lead to different non cell-autonomous behaviors such as (i) proliferation, (ii) directed migration of neighboring cells toward oncogenic cells, and (iii) oncogenic cell extrusion (Figure 8).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5A.

claim: ERK signaling waves lead to oncogenic cell extrusion.
source: Moreover, we showed that sustained ERK activity in oncogenic cells triggers ERK signaling waves through unperturbed neighboring cells. These signaling waves depend on the ADAM17-EGFR paracrine signaling axis and lead to different non cell-autonomous behaviors such as (i) proliferation, (ii) directed migration of neighboring cells toward oncogenic cells, and (iii) oncogenic cell extrusion (Figure 8).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: Cancer mutations can have non-cell autonomous contributions to tissue growth.
source: Our data indicates that cancer mutations can have non-cell autonomous contributions to tissue growth (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4 showing increased proliferation of neighboring cells.

claim: Mosaic oncogene expression promotes proliferation of wild type surrounding cells in mouse epidermis, which is required to expel mutant outgrowths from the tissue.
source: Interestingly, studies in mouse epidermis have shown that mosaic oncogene expression promotes proliferation of wild type surrounding cells, which is required to expel mutant outgrowths from the tissue (Brown et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Brown et al., 2017.

claim: Polypous outgrowths may occur in the presence of non-proliferative oncogenic cells that release growth factors via ADAM17.
source: While the role of ADAM17 in this phenomenon and during early tumorigenesis in vivo is yet unknown, it is tempting to speculate that polypous outgrowths may occur in the presence of non-proliferative oncogenic cells that release growth factors via ADAM17.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed non-cell autonomous proliferation.

claim: Perturbations that elicit sustained ERK activity activate ADAM17, which in turn releases EGFR ligands.
source: Our data suggests that perturbations that elicit sustained ERK activity (eg. B-RafV600E, MEK2DD), activate ADAM17, which in turn releases EGFR ligands (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3 showing ADAM17-dependent AREG release.

claim: The paracrine signal from ADAM17-released EGFR ligands is critical for oncogenic extrusion.
source: This paracrine signal is critical for oncogenic extrusion (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5 showing that blocking this pathway prevents extrusion.

claim: ERK activation drives extrusion to a higher extent than p38 activation.
source: Of note, our data showed that ERK activation drives extrusion to a higher extent than p38 activation (Figure 6), which may result from a difference in overall cell autonomous migration in these two cases (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of extrusion efficiency between ERK and p38 activation in Figure 6.

claim: Sphingosine kinase inhibition caused greater defects in extrusion of p38-active cells than ERK-active cells.
source: Moreover, sphingosine kinase inhibition caused greater defects in extrusion of p38-active cells than ERK-active cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: EDAC of transformed HRASG12V cells is less dependent on sphingosine-1-phosphate production than extrusion of crowded or apoptotic cells.
source: This finding agrees with work showing that EDAC of transformed HRASG12V cells is less dependent on sphingosine-1-phosphate production than extrusion of crowded or apoptotic cells (Yamamoto et al., 2016), where stress signaling may be involved.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yamamoto et al., 2016.

claim: AREG is one of the key EGFR ligands in mammary epithelial cells.
source: We and others have identified AREG as one of the key EGFR ligands in mammary epithelial cells (Sternlicht et al., 2005; Figure 3); however, different ligands may be required in other tissues.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3 and citation to Sternlicht et al., 2005.

claim: Different ligands may be required in other tissues.
source: We and others have identified AREG as one of the key EGFR ligands in mammary epithelial cells (Sternlicht et al., 2005; Figure 3); however, different ligands may be required in other tissues.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about tissue-specific differences.

claim: Local signaling gradients are created by oncogenic cells to coordinate directed migration of neighbors.
source: We propose that local signaling gradients are created by oncogenic cells to coordinate directed migration of neighbors.
evidence: This is proposed based on the observation that disrupting gradients prevents directed migration.

claim: Addition of exogenous AREG or increased fractions of oncogenic cells both prevent directed migration of neighboring cells.
source: To support this idea, we show that addition of exogenous AREG or increased fractions of oncogenic cells both prevent directed migration of neighboring cells (Figure 7), and that during extrusion, polarized actin-containing basal protrusions require growth factor signaling (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 7.

claim: During extrusion, polarized actin-containing basal protrusions require growth factor signaling.
source: To support this idea, we show that addition of exogenous AREG or increased fractions of oncogenic cells both prevent directed migration of neighboring cells (Figure 7), and that during extrusion, polarized actin-containing basal protrusions require growth factor signaling (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Localized ERK signaling gradients have been observed during morphogenesis of Drosophila, avian, and mammalian embryos.
source: Localized ERK signaling gradients have also been observed during morphogenesis of Drosophila, avian, and mammalian embryos (Yang et al., 2002; Ogura et al., 2018; Corson et al., 2003), and in preserving homeostasis of mammalian epidermis and intestinal organoids (Hiratsuka et al., 2015; Muta et al., 2018; Liang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Localized ERK signaling gradients have been observed in preserving homeostasis of mammalian epidermis and intestinal organoids.
source: Localized ERK signaling gradients have also been observed during morphogenesis of Drosophila, avian, and mammalian embryos (Yang et al., 2002; Ogura et al., 2018; Corson et al., 2003), and in preserving homeostasis of mammalian epidermis and intestinal organoids (Hiratsuka et al., 2015; Muta et al., 2018; Liang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hiratsuka et al., 2015; Muta et al., 2018; Liang et al., 2017.

claim: The ADAM17-EGFR paracrine signaling axis may direct collective behaviors during development in addition to roles in oncogenesis.
source: Thus, in addition to roles in oncogenesis, the ADAM17-EGFR paracrine signaling axis may direct collective behaviors during development.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed role in coordinating collective behaviors.

claim: ERK signaling dynamics and the ADAM17-EGFR signaling axis play a critical role in coordinating cell behaviors at the tissue level.
source: Overall, our results highlight the importance of quantitative live-cell approaches to understand the effects of genetic perturbations and cell-cell communication in tissues. We propose a critical role for ERK signaling dynamics and the ADAM17-EGFR signaling axis in coordinating cell behaviors at the tissue level.
evidence: This is the main conclusion proposed based on all experimental findings.
